title: Almost Slipping
sum: A temple singer confesses that he nearly lost his faith. He had been taught that God is good to the pure in heart (73:1), but he saw the arrogant growing fat and rich, mocking God and never sick, while his own clean hands earned him only trouble (73:3–14). He kept his doubts to himself for the sake of God's people (73:15), and the problem wore him down, until he came into God's holy places (73:17).

There he saw two things. The wicked stand on slippery ground and vanish like a dream (73:18–20). And he himself, who had been as dull as an animal, was never let go: "And still I am with you" (73:23). The psalm ends with some of the most loved words in the Psalter: "Who do I have in the heavens?" (73:25) and "Drawing near to God is my good" (73:28). Psalm 73 opens Book III. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 72.
readings: Read as wisdom

The psalm takes up the problem of Job and Ecclesiastes: why the wicked prosper. Its answer is not an argument but a change of view, from looking at the wicked to looking at God. Many scholars class it with the wisdom psalms (1, 37, 49).
Read as a story of faith
It is a personal testimony told in stages: creed (73:1), crisis (73:2–16), turning point in worship (73:17), new sight (73:18–22), new trust (73:23–28). Buber read it as the purifying of a heart.
Read at the center of the Psalter

Walter Brueggemann argued that Psalm 1 states the simple faith that obedience is rewarded, and Psalm 73 tests it in real life and comes out with a deeper faith: God himself is the reward. Placed after Psalm 72's ideal king and at the head of Book III, it opens the Psalter's long struggle with failure.

views.H: Readers who take the title as history hear Asaph, David's chief singer (1 Chronicles 16:5), speaking from his own crisis, perhaps as a Levite with no land or wealth. Jewish and Christian tradition long read the psalm this way.
views.C: Critical scholars read "of Asaph" as the name of a guild of singers and date the psalm loosely, between the late monarchy and the period after the exile. They class it as a wisdom psalm or a psalm of trust. With 74–83 it belongs to the Elohistic Psalter, which prefers "God" to "the LORD". The Hebrew has a few hard places (73:4, 7, 20; see the variants and the note on 73:10). No Dead Sea Scroll copy of Psalm 73 is known. Witnesses in Psalms 73–80. The Hebrew (Leningrad Codex, with its Ketiv/Qere) was read directly for every verse. The Greek readings cited are those of Rahlfs' edition, checked against it. The Syriac, Jerome's two Latin Psalters and the Targum (in Stec's translation) are cited as the editions and commentaries named report them. The Qumran fragments (4QPs-e, 11QPs-b, 11QPs-d and pap6QPs, covering parts of Psalms 76–78) are cited from the published lists, not seen first-hand, and no reading is taken from them. 11QPs-a does not contain these psalms.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 72. Christians pray it in the daily office, and 73:25–26 is used at funerals and in hymns. The Orthodox read it in the tenth kathisma (Psalms 70–76 in Greek numbering).
views.J: Jewish readers have loved 73:23–26 as a word of trust in the face of death. Martin Buber's essay "The Heart Determines" made the psalm famous in modern Jewish thought. Medieval commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak) read 73:24 either as honor in this life or as the soul's reception after death.
views.X: Augustine read the psalm as the soul learning to love God for himself, not for his gifts. Luther and Calvin saw in it the trial of faith when God seems to favor the godless. Many Christians read 73:24 as a hope of glory after death, completed in the resurrection.

deep.b: The psalm turns on a few words. Good opens it (73:1) and closes it (73:28): first "God is good to Israel", finally "drawing near to God is my good". Heart appears six times, from the pure heart of 73:1, to the clean heart that seemed useless (73:13), the soured heart (73:21) and the heart whose rock is God (73:26). The singer's "I" (va'ani) marks each stage (73:2, 22, 23, 28). What changes is not the world. The wicked are as rich at the end as at the beginning. What changes is where the singer stands: in God's holy places, and with his hand held.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a Levite's envy
deep.b: The psalm's images fit a Levite singer unusually well: he owns no land ("my share is God", 73:26, the Levites' portion in Numbers 18:20), he serves in the holy places (73:17), and his words reach the community (73:15). Its temptation may be the specific one of temple servants who depended on the gifts of the rich, watched the rich prosper, and wondered whether their own poverty meant God was not with them. This is a reading of the details, not a known fact about the author; commentators such as Kraus and Goldingay note the Levitical overtones of 73:26 without building on them this far.

echoes: Psalm 1:1–6; Psalm 37:1–40; Psalm 49:15; Job 21:7–13; Jeremiah 12:1–2; Numbers 18:20; Genesis 5:24; Matthew 5:8; James 4:8

settings.what: A testimony of a crisis of faith
settings.by: A singer of Asaph's circle (the title), speaking as "I"
settings.to: God, directly from 73:18 on; but the psalm is spoken in the hearing of the worshiping community, "your children's generation" (73:15)
settings.when: After he has come through his crisis; the turning point was a visit to God's holy places (73:17). Scholars date the psalm between the late monarchy and the years after the exile.
settings.why: To tell the faithful that the prosperity of the wicked is not the last word, and to model honest doubt brought to God rather than spread among his people. It moves the hearer from envy to the discovery that God himself is the good.
settings.readers: For Israelites praying the collected Psalter after the exile, still poor and ruled by others while foreigners and collaborators grew rich, the psalm gave words both for their envy and for their hope.
views: Many read it as one person's real experience (Kraus, Goldingay).
Others read it as a teaching poem in the form of a testimony, written to instruct (Gunkel classed it among the wisdom poems).

traditions.q: Does Psalm 73:24 mean the faithful go to be with God at death?
views: Yes: the souls of the just who die in God's grace, once purified if they need it, see God; the psalm's hope of being "taken" is fulfilled in heaven and finally in the resurrection (Catechism 1023–1030).

Yes: at death the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into the highest heavens, where they wait for the resurrection of their bodies (Westminster Confession 32.1); Calvin read 73:24 of the glory after this life.
Not at death: the dead sleep, unconscious, until the resurrection at Christ's return; "glory" here is that resurrection (Fundamental Beliefs 26).
No: the dead are not conscious; the hope of the faithful is a resurrection, for most to life on a renewed earth.

title: Remember Your Community
sum: The temple has been burned. Enemies roared in God's meeting place, hacked its carved panels with axes and set it on fire (74:3–8). There is no sign and no prophet, and no one knows how long it will last (74:9). The psalm is a communal lament: the people ask why God has pushed them away for good, and urge him to remember the community he bought and Mount Zion where he lived (74:1–2).

At its center stands a hymn (74:12–17). God is the ancient king who split the Sea, crushed the dragons and Leviathan, opened springs and dried rivers, and set up day and night and the seasons. The God who tamed chaos at the beginning is asked to act again, for his own name's sake, against a foolish people that mocks it (74:18–23). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 73.
readings: Read as the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC
Most scholars hear Babylon's destruction of the temple (2 Kings 25:9), and read the psalm beside Lamentations.
Read as the Maccabean crisis
Theodore of Mopsuestia and some modern scholars hear the profanation under Antiochus IV in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:38), especially in the lack of prophets and the "meeting places".
Read as prayer for every ruin
Jews have prayed it for the destruction of 70 AD; Christians for times when churches were burned and the faith mocked. The hymn of 74:12–17 makes it a prayer that the Creator will not let chaos win.

views.H: Readers who hold to an Asaph of David's day read the psalm as prophecy of a future destruction, or assign it to a later singer of Asaph's family (Ezra 2:41), keeping the title as the guild's name.
views.C: Critical scholars date it after 587 BC, a few after 167 BC. They note its shared language with Psalm 79 and Lamentations, and its use of Canaanite combat myth (74:13–14). Several verses are obscure or damaged (74:5, 6, 11); the Greek differs at 74:8, 14 and 19. No Dead Sea Scroll copy of Psalm 74 is known.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 73. In the Orthodox Psalter it is read in the tenth kathisma. Churches and synagogues have often prayed it after disasters to their communities.
views.J: In Jewish tradition the psalm is read as a lament over the destruction of the Temple. Rashi takes "God's meeting places" (74:8) as houses where Israel gathered for prayer.
views.X: The fathers read the burned sanctuary as both the Jerusalem temple and the persecuted church. Calvin weighed the Babylonian and Maccabean settings and taught that the church can pray this psalm in any time of ruin, appealing to God's covenant and honor.

deep.h: The creation hymn at the center
deep.b: Psalm 74 sets a hymn in the middle of a lament. The seven emphatic "you" lines (74:13–17) praise God as the one who defeated the Sea and its monsters and then ordered the world: springs and rivers, day and night, light and sun, borders, summer and winter. The order follows the old Near Eastern pattern, battle then building, that is found in the Babylonian Enuma Elish and the Baal poems from Ugarit. But the psalm turns the pattern into an argument. The temple was meant to be the center of that ordered world. Its destruction looks like chaos winning. So the singer reminds God of his first victory and asks him to win again.

echoes: 2 Kings 25:8–17; Lamentations 2:6–9; Psalm 79:1–13; Isaiah 51:9–10; Isaiah 27:1; Job 41; Exodus 15:13–17; Acts 20:28; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:38–46; Revelation 12:3

settings.what: A communal lament over the burned temple
settings.by: A singer of Asaph's guild, speaking for the community ("us", "our signs"), with a hymn in his own voice ("God is my king", 74:12)
settings.when: After enemies had destroyed and burned the sanctuary and the meeting places in the land, most likely after 587 BC
settings.why: To bring the disaster before God, to remind him of his ownership of the people and his past victories, and to urge him to act for his own name. For the hearers it gave permission to ask "Why?" and "How long?" inside worship, and anchored their hope in God's power as Creator.
settings.readers: Exiles and those left in the ruined land, and the community that rebuilt the temple after 520 BC, prayed it as their own story; later generations prayed it again in 167 BC and after 70 AD.
views: Most scholars (Kraus, Tate, Hossfeld and Zenger).
Theodore of Mopsuestia and a minority of modern scholars.

title: The Cup in the LORD's Hand
sum: A short liturgy of thanks and judgment. The congregation thanks God, whose name is near (75:1). Then God himself speaks: at the time he chooses he will judge fairly; when the earth melts he holds its pillars steady; and he warns the boasters not to raise their horns (75:2–5).

The singer answers: rank does not come from east or west or desert, but from God, who puts one down and lifts another up (75:6–7). The LORD holds a cup of foaming wine, and the wicked must drink it to the dregs (75:8). The psalm ends with praise and a promise to cut off the horns of the wicked (75:9–10). It shares much with Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 74.
readings: Read as a temple liturgy
Gunkel and Mowinckel heard different voices: congregation, prophet speaking for God, and singer. The psalm may have been performed that way at a festival.
Read as an answer to Psalms 73 and 74
After the prosperity of the wicked (73) and the triumph of the enemy (74), God replies: the time is in his hand, and the wicked will drink his cup.

views.H: Readers who take the title strictly hear Asaph the visionary (2 Chronicles 29:30) passing on a word from God.
views.C: Scholars class it as a prophetic liturgy or a communal thanksgiving, of uncertain date. Its parallels with Hannah's song and with Jeremiah's cup of wrath are often noted. The Greek differs at 75:1, 75:5 and 75:9. No Dead Sea Scroll copy of Psalm 75 is known.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 74. The cup of 75:8 became a key image in Christian preaching on judgment and on the cross.
views.J: Rashi and other commentators read the "appointed time" as the time of redemption, and the horns of the wicked as the nations that oppress Israel.
views.X: Christian readers have heard Christ the judge in 75:2 and 75:10, and the cup of 75:8 in the cup Jesus accepted in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36).

echoes: 1 Samuel 2:1–10; Jeremiah 25:15–29; Isaiah 51:17–22; Luke 1:51–53; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 16:19; Mark 14:36

settings.what: A liturgy of thanks with a word from God
settings.by: The congregation (75:1), a speaker in God's name, probably a temple prophet or singer (75:2–5), and the singer (75:6–10)
settings.to: God (75:1, 9); the boasters and the wicked, warned in God's name (75:4–5); the congregation, who hear it all
settings.when: In worship, probably at a festival; the date is unknown
settings.why: To assure worshipers that God has not lost control of the world or of the proud, and to warn the arrogant. The cup image tells the oppressed that the wicked will answer for what they have done, at God's appointed time.
settings.readers: For the community after the exile, ruled by foreign powers, it promised that kingdoms rise and fall at God's word.
views: Gunkel, Mowinckel and many after them.
Others read it as one singer quoting God, without separate voices.

title: God's Lair in Zion
sum: A song of Zion. God is known in Judah, and his lair is in Salem, his den in Zion, like a lion's (76:1–2). From there he broke the weapons of war (76:3). The brave were plundered and fell asleep, and chariot and horse were stunned at his rebuke (76:5–6).

No one can stand before him when he rises to judge, and he does it to save the lowly of the earth (76:7–9). Even human rage ends in his praise (76:10). The psalm closes by calling Israel to keep its vows and the nations to bring gifts to the awesome God (76:11–12). The Greek title links it with the Assyrian army that died outside Jerusalem in 701 BC. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 75.
readings: Read as history
The night the angel of the LORD struck Sennacherib's camp (2 Kings 19:35) fits the sleeping soldiers and stunned horses closely, and the Greek title says so.
Read as a Zion hymn
Like Psalms 46 and 48, it celebrates God's defense of his city, perhaps sung at a festival, without one battle in mind.
Read as the last battle
Some Jewish and Christian readers hear the final defeat of the nations who attack Zion (Zechariah 14; Revelation 20:8–9).

views.H: With the title, an Asaph of David's day could celebrate one of David's victories; most who keep the Greek tradition prefer Hezekiah's day.
views.C: Scholars class it as a Song of Zion, with Psalms 46, 48 and 87, and date it to the monarchy. The lion imagery (76:2) and the name Reshef (76:3) show older poetic roots. The Greek differs at 76:2, 4 and 10 and in the title. A Qumran copy, 4QPs-e (4Q87), preserves 76:10–12 (reported in DJD 16; not seen here).
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 75. It is used at Easter in some Western traditions, where 76:8–9 ("the earth was afraid and went quiet, when God stood up for judgment") was sung of the resurrection.
views.J: Jewish commentators connect it with the defeat of Sennacherib and, looking forward, with the war of Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38–39).
views.X: Christian readers have applied it to Christ's victory over the powers, and to the church as the new Zion.

echoes: 2 Kings 19:32–36; Isaiah 37:33–36; Psalm 46; Psalm 48; Genesis 14:18; Hebrews 7:1–2; Amos 1:2; Exodus 15:1

settings.what: A song of Zion celebrating God's victory
settings.to: The congregation (76:1–3), then God (76:4–10), then Israel and the surrounding peoples (76:11–12)
settings.when: After a deliverance of Jerusalem; the Greek title and many readers say after Sennacherib's army fell (701 BC)
settings.why: To praise God as the defender of Zion and judge of the earth, and to call worshipers to keep the vows they made in danger. It taught that the city's safety lay in God, not in chariots or horses.
settings.readers: After the exile, when Zion had fallen, the psalm became a hope that God would again break the weapons of the nations and save the lowly.
views: The Greek title, Delitzsch and many others.
Kraus, Tate and others read it as a festival hymn of Zion.

title: The Waters Saw You
sum: A sleepless night. The singer cries out to God, stretches out his hands all night, refuses comfort, and finds that remembering God only makes him groan (77:1–4). He thinks of better days and asks six questions that test God's own words: Will the Lord reject forever? Is his loyal love gone? Has he forgotten to be gracious? (77:7–9).

Then he turns (77:10). He decides to remember not his own past but the LORD's deeds, and the psalm becomes a hymn of the exodus: the waters saw God and writhed, thunder and lightning shook the world, and God's way went through the sea though no one saw his footprints. It ends abruptly, with God leading his people like sheep through Moses and Aaron (77:20). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 76.
readings: Read as a personal lament
One person's night of doubt, answered by remembering.
Read as the nation's lament
The "I" may speak for Israel in exile, asking whether the covenant is over, and finding hope in the exodus. Many scholars read it this way.
Read with Habakkuk 3
The theophany at the sea (77:16–19) closely parallels Habakkuk 3:10–15, and both may draw on an older hymn.

views.H: With the title, the psalm is Asaph's own, or his guild's, sung on Jeduthun's instruments or in his style.
views.C: Scholars divide it into a lament (77:1–10) and a hymn (77:11–20), perhaps once separate, and date it to the exile or later. The hymn may be older, related to Habakkuk 3 and Exodus 15. Two Qumran copies preserve parts of it: 4QPs-e (77:1) and 11QPs-b (77:17–20, Hebrew 77:18–21), as reported in DJD 16 and DJD 23.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 76. It is a favorite in times of depression and sleeplessness. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov included it among the ten psalms of his "General Remedy" (Tikkun HaKlali).
views.J: Rashi and other commentators read the speaker as Israel in exile. Jewish readers note the move from "I" to God's deeds as a model of how to pray in darkness.
views.X: Augustine read 77:2–10 as the soul turning inward and then upward. Christian readers link the unseen footprints in the sea with Jesus walking on the water (Mark 6:48–51).

deep.b: The verb "remember" (zakhar) appears in 77:3, 6 and 11. At first, remembering God makes the singer moan (77:3), and remembering "my song in the night" makes him ask whether God has changed (77:6–9). From 77:11 on he remembers differently: not his own happier days, but "the LORD's deeds" and "your wonder of long ago". The same is true of the verb siach, to muse or complain (77:3, 6, 12). The psalm shows the difference between brooding on loss and rehearsing God's acts. It does not deny the darkness. It changes what the mind is fed.

echoes: Exodus 14–15; Exodus 34:6–7; Habakkuk 3:3–15; Isaiah 43:16; Isaiah 51:9–10; Lamentations 3:21–32; Deuteronomy 32:7; Mark 6:48–51

settings.what: A lament that turns into a hymn of the exodus
settings.by: A singer of Asaph's guild, speaking as "I"
settings.to: God ("you" from 77:4 on), in the hearing of the congregation; 77:1–3 and 77:10–12 are spoken about God
settings.when: In a time of long distress, personal or national; many date it to the exile
settings.why: To voice the fear that God has changed, using God's own creed, and to model a way out: remembering what God did at the sea. For the first hearers it said that the God who led Israel through the sea unseen still leads, even when his footprints cannot be seen.
settings.readers: Exiles who wondered whether the covenant had ended found their own questions in 77:7–9 and their answer in the exodus told again in 77:16–20.
views: The community's prayer in the voice of one

title: Tell the Next Generation
sum: The second longest psalm is a sermon in verse on Israel's history, from Egypt to David. The singer calls his people to listen to "riddles from ancient times" so that the next generation will trust God and not be like their stubborn ancestors (78:1–8). Then he tells the story twice. First the wilderness: God split the sea, led them by cloud and fire, and gave water from the rock, manna and quail, but they tested him and he struck them, and they sought him and lied to him, and he forgave them again (78:9–39).

Then he goes back to the start: the plagues on Egypt, the exodus and the gift of the land (78:40–55); but in the land they turned to high places and idols, so God abandoned Shiloh, let the ark be captured and gave his people to the sword (78:56–64). At last the Lord woke up, routed his enemies, rejected Ephraim and chose Judah, Mount Zion and David the shepherd (78:65–72). Matthew 13:35 quotes 78:2. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 77.
readings: Read as teaching
The psalm is a maskil, a wisdom lesson: history told so the young will not repeat it (78:5–8).
Read as an argument for Zion and David
The story builds to the choice of Judah, Zion and David over Ephraim and Shiloh (78:67–72). Clifford and others read it as a defense of the Jerusalem order, perhaps addressed to the north.
Read as a story of grace
Again and again the people sin and God forgives (78:38–39). The psalm ends not with Israel's faithfulness but with God's new beginning.

views.H: Readers who keep the title see Asaph, David's singer, teaching the story up to his own day, which is why it ends with David and says nothing of the divided kingdom or the fall of Samaria.
views.C: Dates proposed range from David's or Solomon's reign (Clifford), to after the split of the kingdom, to Hezekiah's time after 722 BC, to after the exile. Scholars compare its use of the exodus and wilderness traditions with Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy 32 and Judges, and note differences of order and detail (the plagues, 78:43–51). Some think 78:9 is a later gloss. Four Qumran copies preserve parts of the psalm: 4QPs-e (78:6–7, 31–33), 11QPs-b (78:1), 11QPs-d (78:5–12) and pap6QPs (78:36–37), as reported in DJD 16, DJD 23 and DJD 3; no reading is cited from them here.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 77. 78:24–25 ("He gave them heaven's grain") is used in Eucharistic devotion, and Thomas Aquinas's "Panis angelicus" takes up the "bread of angels".
views.J: 78:38 ("Yet he is compassionate") opens the weekday evening service and was recited during the punishment of lashes (Mishnah Makkot 3:14). The Talmud counts it the middle verse of the Psalter (Kiddushin 30a). The Targum and the Talmud connect 78:9 with Ephraimites who left Egypt too early.
views.X: Matthew sees Jesus' parables as the fulfillment of 78:2. John 6:31 quotes a form of 78:24 (compare Exodus 16:4, 15), and Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 10:1–11 draws on the same wilderness stories as a lesson for the church.

deep.h: Psalm 78 beside Exodus, Numbers, Judges and Samuel
deep.b:
Checked against this site's Plain of those books, the psalm follows them closely in substance, with its own order and some details of its own:

  • The sea and the cloud (78:13–14): Exodus 14:21–22; 15:8 ("stood up like a mound"); 13:21.
  • Water from the rock (78:15–16, 20): Exodus 17:6 (a tsur, at Horeb) and Numbers 20:8–11 (a sela', at Kadesh). The psalm uses both words.
  • Testing God (78:18, 41, 56): Exodus 17:7; Numbers 14:22.
  • Fire against Jacob (78:21): Taberah, Numbers 11:1–3.
  • Manna (78:23–25): Exodus 16:4, 13–15, 31; Numbers 11:7–9. The psalm puts it after the rock; Exodus puts it before.
  • Quail and plague (78:26–31): Numbers 11:31–34 (Kibroth Hattaavah), with the east and south winds added. Exodus 16:13 has quail without the plague.
  • Days spent in emptiness (78:33): the forty years of Numbers 14:29–35.
  • Seeking God when struck (78:34): Numbers 21:6–7 and the cycle of Judges 2:18–19.
  • The plagues (78:43–51): seven of Exodus's ten, in a different order (see the note at 78:43).
  • The land shared out (78:55): Joshua 18:8–10, at Shiloh.
  • High places and idols (78:56–58): Judges 2:11–19; 18:30–31.
  • Shiloh, the ark and the priests (78:60–64): 1 Samuel 4:3–22. Shiloh's own fate is not told in Samuel; Jeremiah 7:12 assumes it.
  • The rout of the enemies (78:66): 1 Samuel 5:6–12.
  • David from the sheepfolds (78:70–72): 1 Samuel 16:11; 2 Samuel 7:8.

The psalm leaves out Sinai, the golden calf, the spies' report itself, and the conquest stories, and it never names Moses. Its interest is the pattern: God's gifts, Israel's forgetting, God's anger and God's mercy.
deep.refs: Exodus 13:21; Exodus 15:8; Exodus 16:4; Exodus 17:6–7; Numbers 11:1–34; Numbers 14:22–35; Numbers 20:8–11; Numbers 21:6–7; Judges 2:11–19; 1 Samuel 4:3–22; 2 Samuel 7:8

deep.h: Two rounds of the same story
deep.b: The psalm tells the history in two cycles. Each begins with God's wonders (78:12–16; 78:43–55), moves to Israel's rebellion (78:17–20; 78:56–58) and ends with God's anger and its result (78:21–39; 78:59–64). The first cycle ends in mercy ("Yet he is compassionate", 78:38); the second ends in a new choice (78:65–72). Between them, 78:40–42 says what went wrong: "They did not keep his hand in mind." Forgetting is the psalm's root sin (78:7, 11, 42), and remembering by retelling is its cure (78:4–6).

echoes: Exodus 7–17; Numbers 11; Numbers 14; Numbers 20; Deuteronomy 32; Joshua 18:1–10; Judges 2:11–19; 1 Samuel 4–6; 1 Samuel 16:11; 2 Samuel 7:8; Psalm 105; Psalm 106; Nehemiah 9:9–25; Matthew 13:35; John 6:31; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Acts 7:2–50

settings.what: A teaching psalm retelling Israel's history
settings.by: A teacher-singer of Asaph's guild ("my people ... my teaching")
settings.to: The assembled people of Israel, and through them their children (78:1, 4–6)
settings.when: In worship or instruction, perhaps at a festival; dates proposed range from David's day to after the exile
settings.why: To pass the story to the next generation so that they trust God and do not repeat their ancestors' forgetting, and to explain why God chose Judah, Zion and David after rejecting Shiloh and Ephraim. Knowing it is addressed to all Israel, including the north, sharpens its claim: the place to worship is Zion.
settings.readers: After the exile, when the people had lost land, temple and king, the psalm read as both a warning (they too had forgotten) and a hope: God had begun again before, with Zion and David.
views: A defense of the Davidic order
Clifford dates it to the early monarchy, before the split of the kingdom.
A call to the north after 722 BC
Others read it with Hezekiah's invitation to the north (2 Chronicles 30:6–9).
Some read it as instruction for the restored community.

title: The Nations Have Come In
sum: A lament over Jerusalem in ruins. The nations have entered God's inheritance, defiled the temple, left the bodies of God's servants for the birds, and poured out blood like water with no one to bury it (79:1–3). Israel's neighbors mock (79:4).

The people ask how long God will be angry, and pray that he pour out his fury on the nations that do not know him (79:5–7). They ask him not to count old sins against them, to make atonement for their sins for his name's sake, to avenge the blood of his servants, and to save the prisoners condemned to die (79:8–12). They end with a promise to praise him forever as his flock (79:13). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 78.
readings: Read as 587 BC
Most scholars read it with Lamentations and Psalm 74, after Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem.
Read as the Maccabean age
1 Maccabees 7:17 quotes 79:2–3 of the Hasideans killed in 162 BC, and some scholars think the psalm was written then.
Read as a prayer of martyrs
Revelation's martyrs cry "How long" and ask God to avenge their blood (Revelation 6:10), and Christians have prayed this psalm for persecuted believers.

views.H: Readers who keep the title read it as Asaph's prophecy of Jerusalem's fall, or as a psalm of Asaph's guild after it.
views.C: Scholars date it after 587 BC and note its close links with Psalm 74, Psalm 44:13 (= 79:4) and Jeremiah 10:25 (= 79:6–7). Whether Jeremiah borrowed from the psalm or the psalm from Jeremiah is debated. No Dead Sea Scroll copy of Psalm 79 is known.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 78. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours (1971) prays 79:1–5, 8–11 and 13 (Week III, Thursday, Daytime Prayer), leaving out 79:6–7 and 79:12.
views.J: 79:6–7 is read at the Passover Seder when the door is opened for Elijah. The psalm is also prayed in mourning for the destruction of the Temple.
views.X: Christians have prayed it for the persecuted church; Revelation 6:10 and 19:2 take up its cry for the blood of God's servants. Many Christian readers pray its curses as handing vengeance to God (Romans 12:19).

echoes: 2 Kings 25:8–10; Lamentations 1–2; Psalm 74; Psalm 44:13; Jeremiah 10:25; Deuteronomy 28:26; Deuteronomy 32:43; 1 Maccabees 7:16–17; Revelation 6:10; Revelation 11:9; Revelation 19:2

settings.what: A communal lament over Jerusalem's destruction
settings.by: A singer of Asaph's guild, speaking as "we"
settings.when: After the nations sacked Jerusalem and defiled the temple, most likely after 587 BC, while prisoners were still held and the dead unburied
settings.why: To bring the horror before God and ask him to act: to forgive, to rescue the condemned, and to judge the nations that destroyed his people. It hands vengeance to God. For the hearers it also confessed their own sins (79:8–9) while protesting the cruelty of the enemy.
settings.readers: Survivors in the ruined land and in Babylon, and later the Maccabean generation (1 Maccabees 7:17), heard their own dead in 79:2–3.

traditions.q: Should Christians pray Psalm 79:6–7 and 79:12, the prayers for God's fury on the nations and sevenfold repayment?
views: In the Liturgy of the Hours (1971), Psalm 79 is prayed without 79:6–7 and 79:12, following the rule that some verses with curses are left out of the office (General Instruction 131); the verses remain part of Scripture.

The whole Psalter, Psalm 78 in Greek numbering included, is read in the eleventh kathisma with no verses left out; the fathers read the cursing lines as prayers against sin, the passions and the demons.
Churches that sing only the psalms (Reformed Presbyterian and Free Church tradition) sing Psalm 79 whole, as God-given words that ask God, not the singer, to judge his enemies.
Bonhoeffer taught that such prayers can be prayed only with Christ, who bore God's wrath and prayed for his enemies; so prayed, they hand vengeance to God.

title: Shepherd of Israel
sum: A prayer for the northern tribes in danger. The people call on the Shepherd of Israel, enthroned on the cherubim, to shine out before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh and come to save them (80:1–2). Their refrain, three times and louder each time, asks God to bring them back and make his face shine, the words of the priestly blessing (80:3, 7, 19). They complain that God has fed them tears and made them a laughingstock (80:4–6).

Then comes a parable. Israel is a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted; it filled the land from the Sea to the River (80:8–11). Now its walls are broken and wild boars eat it (80:12–13). The people beg God to turn and tend the vine, to strengthen "the man of your right hand ... the son of man", and they promise not to turn away again (80:14–18). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 79.
readings: Read as the fall of the north
Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, and the Greek title "about the Assyrian", point to the Assyrian attacks of 732–722 BC.
Read as a prayer for all Israel
After the exile the psalm could pray for the reunion of north and south under God the Shepherd.
Read as messianic
The Targum reads the "son" of 80:15 as the King Messiah; Christians hear Jesus, the Son of Man and the true vine.

views.H: With the title, an Asaph of David's day would be praying a prophecy; many who keep the title assign it to Asaph's guild in the late 700s BC.
views.C: Most scholars date it to the last years of the northern kingdom and think it may come from northern circles (Joseph, Ephraim, the cherubim-throne of the ark), later used in Judah. Several think 80:15b was copied from 80:17b. The divine titles grow in the refrain, a careful piece of composition. No Dead Sea Scroll copy of Psalm 80 is known.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 79. It is the responsorial psalm for the First Sunday of Advent in Year B of the Roman and Revised Common Lectionaries and for the Fourth Sunday of Advent in Year C, praying for God's coming: "God, bring us back."
views.J: The Targum reads 80:15 as "the King Messiah". The Talmud notes the suspended ayin of 80:13 (Hebrew 80:14) as the middle letter of the Psalms, and the midrash reads the boar from the forest as Rome.
views.X: Christians read the vine with John 15 and Mark 12:1–9, and "the son of man" whom God made strong as Christ at God's right hand (Mark 14:62). The refrain became an Advent prayer.

deep.b: The refrain appears three times, and each time God's name is fuller: "God" (80:3), "God of Armies" (80:7), "LORD God of Armies" (80:19). Between the second and third comes a shortened form in the middle of the vine parable, "God of Armies, please turn around!" (80:14), using the same verb shuv that is in "bring us back". The prayer turns on that word: the people ask God to bring them back, ask God himself to turn back to them, and promise they will not turn away (80:18). The refrain prays the priestly blessing, "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25), back to God as a plea.

echoes: Genesis 48:15; Genesis 49:22–24; Numbers 6:24–26; Numbers 2:18–24; 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Kings 17:5–6; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 19:10–14; Hosea 10:1; Mark 12:1–9; John 15:1–8; Daniel 7:13; Mark 14:62

settings.what: A communal lament for the northern tribes
settings.by: A singer of Asaph's guild, speaking as "we" for the people
settings.to: God, the Shepherd of Israel enthroned on the cherubim
settings.when: Most likely during the Assyrian attacks on the northern kingdom, 732–722 BC; the Greek title says "about the Assyrian"
settings.why: To ask God to come to the rescue of Joseph's tribes, appealing to his past care (the vine from Egypt), and to promise renewed faithfulness. If prayed in Judah, it was a prayer for the brother tribes of the north, a sign that the south still counted them as God's people.
settings.readers: After the exile, with the northern tribes long scattered, the psalm became a prayer for the restoration of all Israel under God.
views: Prayed in the north before 722 BC
Prayed in Judah for the north
Others, noting it was kept in Jerusalem's collection.
